title: Two heaps
summary: Split the values into a lower half in a max-heap and an upper half in a min-heap. Keep the sizes within one, and the median is always at the tops.
idea: The largest of the small half and the smallest of the large half sit at the two roots, so the middle is O(1) to read.

signals.see: You need the median, or another middle value, after every insert in a stream.
signals.think: Use a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Rebalance so their sizes differ by at most 1.

signals.see: You must keep choosing the best option among those that have become available, such as the most profitable affordable project.
signals.think: Keep one heap of locked options sorted by cost, and move them into a second heap sorted by value once you can afford them.

signals.see: Each item needs the nearest item past some threshold, and both lists can be processed in sorted order.
signals.think: Put both sides in min-heaps and pop them together, like two sorted queues.

phrasings: Response times arrive one by one. After each one, report the median so far.
With some starting money, pick up to k projects one at a time to end with the most money.
For each meeting, find the next meeting that starts no earlier than this one ends.

picture.title: The median lives between two roots
picture.alt: On the left, the whole list is sorted again after each new value to read the middle, at O(n log n) each time. On the right, a max-heap holds the lower half and a min-heap the upper half; each value costs O(log n), and the median is read from the two roots.
picture.caption: Keep the halves balanced, and the median is always at the tops.

code.py:
import heapq

def running_median(nums):
    low, high, medians = [], [], []  #@init
    for x in nums:
        if not low or x <= -low[0]:  #@choose
            heapq.heappush(low, -x)
        else:
            heapq.heappush(high, x)
        if len(low) > len(high) + 1:  #@balance
            heapq.heappush(high, -heapq.heappop(low))
        elif len(high) > len(low):
            heapq.heappush(low, -heapq.heappop(high))
        medians.append(-low[0] if len(low) > len(high) else (-low[0] + high[0]) / 2)  #@median
    return medians  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 10 whole numbers between -99 and 99, separated by commas or spaces.

oneLiner: low = max-heap, high = min-heap; add to one, move a top across if sizes differ by 2

exercise.prompt: intervals[i] is [start, end], and every start is different. For each interval, return the index of the interval with the smallest start that is greater than or equal to its end, or -1 if there is none. An interval may be its own answer when start equals end. Pop the ends in order from one min-heap and discard starts that are too early from another. The starter discards a start that equals the end, so exact touches are missed.
hints: Put (start, index) pairs in one min-heap and (end, index) pairs in another.
Pop ends from smallest up. A start that is too early for this end is too early for every later end, so it can be thrown away for good.

complexity.why: Each value is pushed into one heap and moved across at most once, so each insert costs O(log n). Reading the median only looks at the two roots, which is O(1).

mistakes: Putting the lower half in a min-heap. Its largest value, the one next to the median, would be buried.
Forgetting to rebalance, so one heap grows much bigger and the tops no longer straddle the middle.
Comparing a new value with the wrong top, which puts it in the wrong half.
Using integer division for the average of the two tops when the median can be a half.

quiz.question: Which heap holds the lower half of the values?
choices: A min-heap, so its smallest value is on top
A max-heap, so its largest value is on top
quiz.explain: The value next to the median in the lower half is its largest, so the lower half must be a max-heap.

quiz.question: After an insert, low holds 4 values and high holds 2. What should happen?
quiz.explain: The sizes may differ by at most one. Moving low's largest value across keeps both halves in order.

quiz.question: low holds 3 values and high holds 3. Where is the median?
choices: The average of the two tops
quiz.explain: With an even count, the median is halfway between the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half.

interviewTip: Draw the two halves as a valley: the max-heap's top on the left, the min-heap's top on the right, and the median between them. State the size rule before you code.
